name: Chamikuro
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.
catalog_citation: Parker, Steve. 2022. Apuntes sobre la Gramática del Chamikuro (Notes on Chamikuro Grammar). Occasional Papers in Applied Linguistics 14. Dallas International University. PDF:https://www.diu.edu/documents/OPAL/No-14-Parker-Apuntes-sobre-la-gram%C3%A1tica-del-…
catalog_quote: 2.2 Acentuación El acento fonético primario siempre cae en la penúltima sílaba de cada palabra, con una regularidad extrema. ... Dato curioso: entre más de tres mil palabras individuales, sólo encontré un par de excepciones, y son préstamos del castellano. Entre las palabras nativas jamás he encontrado excepciones.

new_statements.quote: p. 37: "Como ya se ha visto, el chamicuro tiene una regla muy consistente de acentuación en la penúltima sílaba. Sólo se han encontrado unas cuantas excepciones y éstas constituyen préstamos del castellano. Las palabras nativas del chamicuro siempre terminan en vocal, de modo que la regla podría escribirse tal como sigue: (22) Asignación del Acento I [...] Ejemplos: /menu/ [ménu] 'lengua' /tinawa/ [tináwa] 'brazo' /kantis/ [káncis] 'siete'". p. 35: "El chamicuro tiene una regla muy consistente de acentuación en la penúltima sílaba. La única excepción a esta regla se presenta cuando se reduplica una vocal después de una /?/ que se encuentra en la penúltima sílaba, p. ej. [tú?ulu] 'pecho' (/tu?lu/)."
new_statements.translation: p. 37: "As has already been seen, Chamicuro has a very consistent rule of stress on the penultimate syllable. Only a few exceptions have been found, and these are loanwords from Spanish. Native Chamicuro words always end in a vowel, so the rule could be written as follows: (22) Stress Assignment I [...] Examples: /menu/ [ménu] 'tongue', /tinawa/ [tináwa] 'arm', /kantis/ [káncis] 'seven'." p. 35: "Chamicuro has a very consistent rule of stress on the penultimate syllable. The only exception to this rule occurs when a vowel is reduplicated after a /ʔ/ that is in the penultimate syllable, e.g. [túʔulu] 'chest' (/tuʔlu/)."
new_statements.citation: [NOT in the listed works; related open copy already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 pass] Parker, Stephen G. 1991. Estudios sobre la fonología del Chamicuro (Serie Lingüística Peruana 30; 2a ed. 2008). Lima: Ministerio de Educación / Instituto Lingüístico de Verano. First study = Spanish translation of Parker's 1988 UT Arlington MA thesis 'Some universal aspects of coalescence processes confirmed by Chamicuro phonology and morphology'.
new_statements.locator: printed p. 37 (= p. 37), section 'Acento', rules (22)-(23); also p. 35 'Reduplicación vocálica' and p. 25 'Las consonantes glotales'
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (218 pp, the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Estudios sobre la fonología del chamicuro') and rendered PDF page 37 to an image: header 'LOS PROCESOS DE COALESCENCIA 37', section 'Acento', so p. 37 = printed p. 37 as stated. The p. 37 passage is on the page verbatim: 'Como ya se ha visto, el chamicuro tiene una regla muy consistente de acentuación en la penúltima sílaba. Sólo se han encontrado unas cuantas excepciones y éstas constituyen préstamos del castellano. Las palabras nativas del chamicuro siempre terminan en vocal, de modo que la regla podría escribirse tal como sigue: (22) Asignación del Acento I V → [+acento] / ___ C0 (V) #', then '(23) Asignación del Acento II V → [+acento]…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog penultimate stress (penult). Adds: exceptions limited to Spanish loans; surface antepenult only in echo-vowel forms (derived by rule ordering); native words vowel-final and minimally disyllabic; length contrastive but not stress-relevant.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (underlying) word, counted without regard to vowel length or syllable closure; native words are always vowel-final and at least disyllabic. Rule (23) Stress Assignment II extends the same penult count to consonant-final Spanish loans.
new_statements.exceptions: (a) A few Spanish loanwords (p. 37). (b) Words with an optional echo vowel copied after /ʔ/ (Vowel Reduplication) surface with antepenultimate stress, e.g. [túʔulu] 'pecho', [tʃikíʔina] 'estrecho', because Vowel Reduplication is ordered after Stress Assignment (pp. 25, 35-36); p. 25 states these are 'the only words that show stress on the antepenultimate syllable'. Vowel length is contrastive (p. 36-37) but plays no role in the stress rule.
new_statements.identity_note: Both works are by the same author on the same variety: Chamicuro of Pampa Hermosa (Huallaga river, Loreto, Peru), the sole remaining community; Parker 1991 (p. 12) notes the language was already in the process of extinction. No dialect distinction is made.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim in the Parker 2022 text we hold at sec. 2.2, pp. 3-4. (2) The deciding source is a 14-pp grammar sketch (2022) by the language's sole field linguist; the best available work is his 218-pp phonology monograph Parker 1991 (SLP 30), Glottolog's top phonology entry, which we did not hold.
